items.title: How Chess Opening Names Actually Get Assigned
items.content_text: Chess openings get named after players, cities, or eras, then standardized by ECO codes so databases can reference the same line consistently.

items.title: How Nicknames Actually Take Hold in a Culture
items.content_text: Most nicknames fade within weeks. The ones that stick share a repeatable pattern: repetition, a good origin story, and social status.

items.title: How Peer Review Actually Works in Academic Publishing
items.content_text: Before publication, an editor screens a paper and anonymous experts scrutinize its methods. The system catches errors, but has documented, well-studied limits.

items.title: How Pigments Were Actually Sourced Before Synthetic Dyes
items.content_text: Ultramarine cost more than gold and Tyrian purple took thousands of crushed snails per gram, so pigment cost directly decided which colors artists could use.

items.title: How Standardized Test Scores Actually Get Scaled
items.content_text: Raw scores aren't reported directly. Test-makers equate and scale them so a score means the same thing across different test versions and years.

items.title: How Universities Actually Calculate GPA and Class Rank
items.content_text: GPA is a credit-weighted average of grade points, not a simple mean of letter grades. Weighted GPA and class rank each add their own layer on top.

items.title: How Video Game Save Files Actually Work
items.content_text: A save file is a snapshot of game state variables, not the game itself. Manual saves, autosaves, and checkpoints each write that snapshot differently.

items.title: The Legend of Baba Yaga
items.content_text: Baba Yaga is a Slavic folklore witch who lives in a hut on chicken legs, and she's never simply good or evil. Here's who she actually is.

items.title: The Legend of the Pied Piper of Hamelin
items.content_text: In 1284, Hamelin's town chronicle recorded that its children vanished. Here's what the earliest sources say, and the leading theories for what really happened.

items.title: The Legend of the Yeti and Why It Persists
items.content_text: DNA testing has traced yeti hair samples to bears, not an unknown primate. Here's why the legend still persists despite each debunking.

items.title: The Real History Behind the Legend of Mulan
items.content_text: Mulan comes from a Chinese poem written around the 5th-6th century, far sparser than modern retellings. Historians still debate if she was real.

items.title: Why Cramming Feels Effective but Rarely Works
items.content_text: Rereading notes right before a test creates a false sense of mastery. Cognitive psychology calls it the fluency illusion, and it rarely holds up on the actual exam.

items.title: Why Egg Tempera Was Used Before Oil Paint
items.content_text: Egg tempera dried in minutes and forced thin hatched brushwork; oil paint's slow drying let painters blend, which is why it displaced tempera.

items.title: Why Group Brainstorming Produces Fewer Ideas Than Alone
items.content_text: Studies find group brainstorming generates fewer ideas than the same people working alone, largely due to production blocking.

items.title: Why Handshake Customs Differ So Much Around the World
items.content_text: The handshake likely began as proof of an empty weapon hand. Grip, duration, and whether to shake at all still vary sharply by culture.

items.title: Why Laugh Tracks Are Still Used in Some TV Shows
items.content_text: Added laughter measurably makes audiences rate content as funnier, a finding from the same 1950s device that still shapes some sitcoms today.

items.title: Why Players House-Rule Board Games So Often
items.content_text: Most groups quietly change a board game's official rules. Ambiguous wording, perceived balance issues, and family habit all drive the practice.

items.title: Why Self-Portraits Became a Distinct Genre
items.content_text: Better mirrors and a free, always-available model turned rare self-portrait cameos into a full Renaissance genre used for skill display and self-promotion.

items.title: Why Some Cultures Use Patronymics Instead of Surnames
items.content_text: A patronymic is built fresh each generation from the father's first name, unlike a fixed surname. It still causes real problems for modern paperwork.

items.title: Why Some Sculptures Are Left Deliberately Unfinished
items.content_text: Some sculptures were left visibly emerging from raw stone on purpose. This 'non finito' choice is famous in Michelangelo's work, not abandonment.
